title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: GAR 3 — actus vs habitus / Thes. 24
pass_a_gloss: GAR. 3. Finally just as those acts by which a habit is acquired are not themselves the acquisition of the habit, but acquisition follows upon them: so also the acts by which a habit is shaken off are not themselves the privation of the habit, but that privation follows upon them. In vain therefore does the Learned Man boast in his Theses on the state of fallen man before Grace, Th. 24: that we are deprived of justice by this very [fact], that we transgress the law, and that by this very change by which corruption was introduced into Adam, justice was expelled from the same. For if he understands transgression of the law to be the meritorious cause of privation of justice, we easily grant it. If he thinks transgression of the law and privation of justice differ nothing at all between themselves, we do not approve: because transgression of the law is an action, privation of justice is a passion: but to suffer and to act differ more than in words: And God creates men's souls destitute of the ornament of original justice, who yet by creating does not make them transgressors of the law. So expulsion of justice is antecedent to corruption, and corruption consequent to expulsion of justice: but antecedent and consequent differ somewhat between themselves, as I suppose: And God stripped man of the gifts granted in creation, whom yet he did not corrupt.
pass_b_english: Garissoles' third reason. Acts that build a habit are not themselves the acquiring of the habit—acquisition follows them. Likewise acts that shake a habit off are not themselves the privation—privation follows them. So Placeus boasts in vain in his Theses on fallen man before grace (Th. 24): that we lose righteousness by the very fact that we break the law, and that the change which brought corruption into Adam itself expelled righteousness from him.

If he means law-breaking is the meritorious cause of losing righteousness, we grant it. If he thinks law-breaking and privation of righteousness differ not at all, we refuse: breaking the law is an action; privation is a passion; acting and suffering differ more than in words. God creates souls without the ornament of original righteousness yet does not, by creating, make them law-breakers. Expulsion of righteousness precedes corruption; corruption follows expulsion—antecedent and consequent differ. God stripped man of creation's gifts yet did not corrupt him.
source_text: GAR. 3. Denique sicut actus illi, quibus habitus comparatur, non sunt ipsa habitus acquisitio, sed ad eos consequitur acquisitio: ita etiam actus, quibus excutitur habitus, non sunt ipsa habitus privatio, sed ad eos consequitur illa privatio. Frustra ergo jactat Vir Doctus in Thesibus suis de statu hom. Lapsi ante Grat. Th. 24. Nos hoc ipso justitia privari, quod legem transgredimur, & hac ipsa mutatione, qua corruptio introducta est in Adamum, ab eodem expulsam esse justitiam. Etenim si intelligit transgressionem legis esse causam meritoriam privationis justitiae, facile agnoscimus. Si putat transgressionem legis & privationem justitiae nihil inter se differre omnino, non probamus: quia transgressio legis est actio, privatio justitiae passio est: at pati & agere plusquam verbis differunt: Et Deus animas hominum creat justitia originalis decoramento destitutas, qui tamen creando non facit legis praevaricatrices. Sic expulsio justitiae est antecedens ad corruptionem, & corruptio consequens ad expulsionem justitiae: antecedens autem & consequens, nonnihil differunt inter se, ut opinor: Et Deus hominem concessis creatione donis spoliavit, quem tamen non corrupit.
